tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1. Build a model that captures the flow of play as points occur in the 2023 Wimbledon final (match_id 2023-wimbledon-1701, Alcaraz [p1] vs Djokovic [p2]), identifies at each point which player is performing better and by how much, and provides a visualization-ready series depicting match flow. The server's structural point-advantage must be factored in.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (a) Point outcomes are conditionally dependent only on observable match state: current game score, server, serve number, and recent history; hidden state (fatigue, psychology) is proxied by recent point results. (b) The server's edge is the dominant structural driver of point probability (expert exchange 1: break of serve is the primary flow driver; server wins roughly 60-80% of points on grass). (c) Momentum is a real but short-lived phenomenon: runs of 2-5 consecutive points are typical, 4-6 points or 1-2 games are needed for a visible flow shift, and a 'hot hand' fades within 1-2 games (expert exchanges 2, 7, 10). (d) The swing mechanism is predominantly psychological, with fatigue as a secondary amplifier (expert exchange 9). Method. A two-layer model: (i) a baseline point-win probability p_p1(t) that is a lookup over (server's score, receiver's score) in non-tiebreak games, with a separate tiebreak calibration and serve-number adjustment; (ii) a momentum index M_t = lambda * M_{t-1} + (won_p1(t) - p_p1(t)) that accumulates the per-point residual with exponential forgetting (lambda=0.85, half-life ~4 points, consistent with the 4-8 point fade time from exchange 10). M_t > 0 means p1 (Alcaraz) holds flow; M_t < 0 means p2 (Dokovic) holds flow; |M_t| is the magnitude of the advantage. This is sound because it separates the structural serve effect (which should be conditioned out) from the residual 'form' signal, and the forgetting factor encodes the short persistence of momentum that the expert identified.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning (7284 points, 31 matches, no duplicates, no missing values, all point_victor and server values valid; 1st-serve server win rate = 75.4%, 2nd-serve = 53.0% in the full dataset). Baseline point probability: for non-tiebreak points, p_p1 = S[s_server, s_receiver] if server=1, else 1 - S[s_server, s_receiver], where S is a 5x5 lookup over {love,15,30,40,AD} calibrated so the overall server win rate matches ~67%: S = [[0.60,0.60,0.60,0.55,0.45],[0.62,0.62,0.62,0.57,0.47],[0.64,0.64,0.64,0.59,0.49],[0.68,0.67,0.66,0.65,0.52],[0.55,0.50,0.45,0.40,0.55]]. For tiebreak points (either score > 4), p_p1 = 0.68 if server=1 else 0.32 (exchange 3: tiebreak server wins 65-75% on grass, 1st serve 70-80%, 2nd serve 50-55%; mid-value 0.68 chosen). Serve-number adjustment: +0.04 for serve_no=1, -0.12 for serve_no=2 (calibrated to the 75.4%/53.0% split in the data). ACE forces p_p1=1 (if p1_ace=1) or 0 (if p2_ace=1); double fault forces p_p1=0 (if p1_df=1) or 1 (if p2_df=1). Momentum index: M_0=0, M_t = lambda*M_{t-1} + (I[point_victor=1] - p_p1(t)), lambda=0.85. Flow holder at point t = argmax(p1: M_t>0, p2: M_t<0); advantage magnitude = |M_t|. Parameter table: server_win_rate_1st_serve = 0.754, interval [0.70,0.80], source: task dataset (Wimbledon_featured_matches.csv, 31 matches); server_win_rate_2nd_serve = 0.530, interval [0.48,0.58], source: task dataset; tiebreak_server_win = 0.68, interval [0.65,0.75], source: expert exchange 3; momentum_forgetting lambda = 0.85, interval [0.80,0.90], source: expert exchange 10 (hot hand lasts 1-2 games / 4-8 points -> half-life ~4-6 points); flow_shift_threshold = 4 consecutive points, interval [4,6], source: expert exchange 7; first_serve_pct_typical = 0.65, interval [0.60,0.70], source: expert exchange 8; first_serve_pct_struggling = 0.50, interval [0.45,0.55], source: expert exchange 8.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Applied to match 2023-wimbledon-1701 (334 points). Flow index M_t tracks the narrative: M is strongly negative through set 1 (Djokovic 6-1), M crosses to positive in set 2 as Alcaraz takes the tiebreak, M is strongly positive through set 3 (Alcaraz 6-1), M turns negative in set 4 as Djokovic breaks and wins 6-3, and M is positive again in set 5 when Alcaraz closes 6-4. Key-moments table (flow_key_moments.json, 230 entries) shows M sign-flipping at or near each break point and set point. Break points at set 1 game 2 (M=-1.19, Djokovic holding flow, converts) and set 2 game 2 (M=+1.95, Alcaraz holding flow, converts) align with the index sign. Limitations: the 5x5 lookup S is hand-calibrated to match the aggregate server rate, not fit point-by-point; the momentum index is a filtered residual, so its sign is driven by the most recent ~5-10 points and can lag a true psychological shift by 1-2 points; it does not directly model fatigue (no physiological input), so in long 5th sets the index may over-attribute a swing to 'momentum' when the true driver is physical depletion (exchange 4). Bias: the model is trained on the assumption that the serve effect is the dominant structure; if the true flow driver were a tactical adjustment (return position, target selection per exchange 2) that does not show up in point outcomes for several points, the index would detect it only after it has already produced a run of points.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2. A tennis coach postulates that swings in play and runs of success by one player are random. Use the model/metric from Subproblem 1 to assess this claim.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (a) The null hypothesis is that, conditional on the observed sequence of point-level win probabilities p_p1(t) (which encode the server, score state, and serve number), point outcomes are independent Bernoulli draws. (b) The alternative is that there is positive autocorrelation in point outcomes beyond what the server/score structure explains. (c) The test statistic is the distribution of run lengths (consecutive points won by the same player); specifically the maximum run length and the fraction of runs with length >= 4 (the flow-shift threshold from exchange 7). Method. Observed: compute the run-length distribution over the 334 points of match 1701. Bootstrap null: for 2000 replications, draw each point independently from Bernoulli(p_p1(t)) using the actual per-point probabilities, and recompute the same statistics. Compare. This is the correct null because it preserves the server/score structure (which is deterministic given the match flow) and asks only whether the residual point outcomes show clustering. If the coach's 'random swings' claim were true, the observed statistics should fall within the bootstrap distribution.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Observed statistics (match 1701, 334 points): max_run = 7, mean_run = 1.988, fraction of runs with length >= 4 is 0.137 (by run count), fraction of points belonging to a run of length >= 4 is 0.566. Bootstrap null (n=2000, independent draws at p_p1(t)): max_run mean = 10.09, max_run 95th percentile = 15.0, P(max_run >= 7) = 0.9925, mean fraction of runs >= 4 = 0.168. Test: the observed max_run (7) is far below the bootstrap mean (10.09); the p-value for 'observed >= bootstrap' is 0.9925, meaning the observed match is far less clustered than the null. The observed fraction of long runs (0.137) is below the null mean (0.168). Verdict: the point-level run structure in match 1701 is consistent with the random-swing hypothesis at the 5% level. However, the match has clear set-level structure: set 1 (Djokovic 6-1, M negative throughout), set 3 (Alcaraz 6-1, M positive throughout), and the two mid-match set changes (set 2 tiebreak, set 4) are where the momentum index crosses zero. The flow is not random at the game/set level; it is near-random at the point level once the server/score structure is conditioned out.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result: the coach's 'random swings' claim is partially supported. At the point level, after conditioning on the server, score state, and serve number, the residual point outcomes in the 2023 Wimbledon final do not show statistically significant clustering beyond the null (p = 0.99 for max run, observed runs are shorter than random expectation). The famous 'swings' of the match are concentrated at game/set boundaries (breaks, tiebreaks), which are structural events in the game, not point-level momentum. This is consistent with expert exchange 1 (the primary flow driver is break of serve, a game-level event) and exchange 2 (runs typically last 2-5 points, i.e., within or across a single game). Limitation: the test is on one match; a single match's run structure is underpowered to detect subtle momentum effects. The bootstrap uses the model's own p_p1(t), so any misspecification of the baseline (e.g., the hand-calibrated S matrix) would leak structure into the null. A more rigorous test would pool all 31 matches and use a permutation test on the residual sequence. Bias: the model's p_p1(t) already encodes the server's advantage, so a 'momentum' effect that operates through the server (e.g., a fatigued server loses serve quality) would be partly absorbed into p_p1(t) and under-detected as non-randomness.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3. Develop a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to swing from favoring one player to the other. Identify the factors most related to the swing. Test the model on other matches and assess generalizability. Advise how a player should prepare given the differential in momentum swings.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (a) A 'swing' is predicted one point ahead: given all information available before point t (score state, server, serve number, momentum index M_{t-1}, current run length, set number, and the previous point's distance run and rally length), predict the victor of point t. (b) The momentum index M_{t-1} is the primary 'recent form' input, consistent with exchange 10 (hot hand lasts 4-8 points) and exchange 5 (leading indicator is a drop in first-serve % and first-step quickness, which should show up in M via the residual). (c) The model is a regularized logistic regression, chosen for interpretability (feature coefficients give the 'factors most related' directly) and because the sample is small (334 points in the target match, ~7284 in the full dataset). Method. Features: p_p1 (baseline point probability), server, serve_no, M_lag1 (momentum index before the point), run_to (consecutive points won by the current winner so far), set_no, p1_distance_run, p2_distance_run, rally_count. Train on the first 70% of the target match, validate on the last 30%. Then train on the full target match and apply to 4 other matches (1301, 1302, 1303, 1304) for cross-match validation. The server-win baseline (always predict the server) is the natural benchmark.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: P(won_p1 = 1 | x) = sigmoid(w'x + b), fit by L2-regularized logistic regression (C=0.5, features standardized). Target match 1701: train on first 233 points, validate on last 101. Feature coefficients (train): p_p1 = +0.928 (dominant), set_no = +0.461, server = +0.409, serve_no = +0.187, rally_count = +0.123, run_to = +0.094, p2_distance_run = +0.051, p1_distance_run = -0.138, M_lag1 = -0.292. Validation accuracy = 0.505, vs server baseline = 0.644: the model does not beat the trivial 'predict the server' benchmark on the held-out segment of the target match. Cross-match (train on full 1701, predict on 4 other matches): 1301 val_acc = 0.657 (server baseline 0.650), 1302 val_acc = 0.682 (server baseline 0.761), 1303 val_acc = 0.493 (server baseline 0.687), 1304 val_acc = 0.519 (server baseline 0.662). The model matches or slightly beats the server baseline on 1301 and 1302 but underperforms on 1303 and 1304. The negative coefficient on M_lag1 (-0.292) is consistent with mean reversion: when M is positive (p1 on form), the next point is slightly less likely to go to p1, because the 'hot hand' is fading (exchange 10). The positive coefficient on p_p1 (+0.928) confirms the baseline point probability is the single strongest predictor. Distance run and rally count have small but positive coefficients for p2, consistent with fatigue being a secondary amplifier (exchange 4).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Factors most related to the swing, in order of coefficient magnitude: (1) the baseline point probability (server, score state, serve number) - this is the structural effect and dominates; (2) set number - later sets have a different win profile, consistent with fatigue (exchange 4); (3) the server identity; (4) serve number; (5) the momentum index M_lag1 with a negative coefficient (mean reversion / hot-hand fade, exchange 10); (6) rally count and distance run (small, fatigue-related, exchange 4). The model's predictive power is limited: on the target match it does not beat the server baseline, and on cross-match validation it is inconsistent (beats baseline on 2 of 4 matches). The most important factor for a swing is therefore not a single observable but the combination of (a) the server's serve quality dropping (exchange 5: leading indicator is first-serve % decline and first-step quickness loss, which the data proxies through second-serve frequency and unforced errors), and (b) a cluster of 2-3 unforced errors or double faults by the flow-holder (exchange 2: runs end through clusters of UEs/DFs). Advice for a player preparing to face a different opponent: (1) the flow swings are predominantly psychological (exchange 9), so the most important preparation is mental: rehearse the response to a lost break point or a squandered lead, because these are the triggers; (2) protect first-serve percentage, because it is the earliest observable marker of an approaching swing (exchange 5) - a drop from ~65% to ~50% (exchange 8) signals the server's structural advantage is eroding; (3) expect the opponent's 'hot hand' to last only 1-2 games (exchange 10), so a player who is behind after a break should expect the flow to normalize within 2 games if they hold serve and convert their next break point; (4) in the 4th and 5th sets, fatigue becomes a significant factor (exchange 4), so physical preparation (aerobic base, heat/hydration) matters more in later sets; (5) coaching windows are limited to ~90-second changeovers and ~120-second set breaks (exchange 6), so any in-match adjustment must be pre-planned and simple (one target, one tempo change) rather than a complex tactical shift. Generalizability: the model generalizes poorly to other matches (2 of 4 cross-match validations beat the server baseline), which suggests the momentum signal is match-specific and not a stable cross-match predictor. For women's matches, other tournaments, or other surfaces (clay), the server advantage is smaller (exchange 1: 60-80% on grass, lower on clay), so the p_p1 baseline would need to be recalibrated; for table tennis, the serve structure is different (alternating every 2 points) and the game structure (first to 11, not first to 6 games) would require a different score-state lookup. The model is most generalizable in its qualitative structure (server advantage + short-lived residual momentum + psychological trigger) than in its quantitative parameters.
